Before an unvoiced k the visarga simply stays. Contrast the next junction.

samasa.vigraha: संसारस्य स्थितिः संसारस्थितिः; तां करोति इति संसारस्थितिकारी, तेन
samasa.type: upapada tatpuruṣa (the agent noun कारिन्, kṛt -in, after its object) containing a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa (संसारस्थिति)
samasa.sense: which keeps the round of birth and death going

samasa.type: karmadhāraya (avadhāraṇa: the first member identified with the second)
samasa.sense: Viṣṇu’s sleep between ages, which is not ignorance but withdrawn absorption
samasa.alt: Also read as a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa, योगस्य निद्रा, ‘the sleep of yoga’; the sense is the same.

samasa.literal: of the lord of the world

morph.note: Gerundive of √कृ with ṇyat: कृ + य → कार्य (vṛddhi of the root vowel). With न it expresses what ought not to be: विस्मयः न कार्यः ‘wonder is not to be made’ = ‘do not wonder’.
Instrumental singular of an -in stem: कारिन् + आ → कारिणा (n → ṇ after r). It agrees with प्रभावेण, not with महामाया: it is the power that keeps saṃsāra in place.

mantras.anvaya: (ते) संसारस्थितिकारिणा महामायाप्रभावेण (ममतावर्ते मोहगर्ते निपातिताः)। तत् अत्र विस्मयः न कार्यः। (एषा) जगत्पतेः योगनिद्रा …
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line completes the sentence of 1.53 (‘they are thrown into the whirlpool of mine-ness … by the power of Mahāmāyā’). Then a short main clause with a gerundive (विस्मयः न कार्यः), and the opening of a new sentence that 1.55 completes (योगनिद्रा जगत्पतेः … एषा).
mantras.lit: (They are thrown down) by the power of Mahāmāyā, which makes the continuance of saṃsāra. Therefore no wonder is to be felt in this: the yogic sleep of the lord of the world —
mantras.tr: It is the power of Mahāmāyā, who keeps the round of worldly existence turning, that casts them down. So there is nothing to wonder at here. She who is the yogic sleep of the Lord of the world —
mantras.tr_note: The first line ends the sentence of 1.53; the last words begin the sentence completed in 1.55.

comm.t: The sage Medhas answers the king’s question (1.44–45: why are we attached when we see the fault?). Creatures who know better are still bound to their own, as the birds feeding their young show (1.51–53); the cause is the power of Mahāmāyā, so it is no cause for surprise. In the digital text a footnote asterisk of the printed book followed संसारस्थितिकारिणा; it has been removed (corrections.json, encoding).

The answer turns a psychological question into a theological one: attachment is not merely a private failure but the working of the power that keeps the world in being. The same Goddess is introduced in the same breath as Viṣṇu’s Yoganidrā, the name under which Brahmā will praise her (1.69–71).

samasa.sense: the Goddess as the power that veils and binds
samasa.alt: As a name it can also be taken as a bahuvrīhi, महती माया यस्याः सा ‘she whose māyā is great’; the karmadhāraya fits the identification with Yoganidrā better.

morph.note: Passive of a causative: मोहय- loses its causative -ay- before the passive -ya- (मोह् + य + ते). The world is the subject; तया names the agent: ‘the world is deluded by her’.
Neuter plural of चेतस्: the s-stems insert a nasal and lengthen the vowel in the nominative and accusative plural (चेतांसि, like मनांसि). Here accusative, looking forward to the verbs of 1.56.

mantras.anvaya: (या) जगत्पतेः योगनिद्रा, एषा हरेः महामाया च; तया जगत् सम्मोह्यते। सा हि भगवती देवी ज्ञानिनाम् अपि चेतांसि (बलात् आकृष्य मोहाय प्रयच्छति)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line identifies the Yoganidrā of 1.54 with Hari’s Mahāmāyā and states her work with a passive (तया सम्मोह्यते जगत्). The second line begins a sentence completed in 1.56: चेतांसि is the object of आकृष्य … प्रयच्छति there, and देवी भगवती हि सा is a parenthesis giving the reason.
mantras.lit: — and this one is the Mahāmāyā of Hari; by her the world is deluded. The minds even of the wise — for she is the Goddess, the Blessed One —
mantras.tr: — she is Hari’s Great Māyā, and by her the whole world is held in delusion. Even the minds of the wise — for she is the Goddess, the Blessed Lady —
mantras.tr_note: The sentence is carried over from 1.54 and into 1.56, where the verbs governing चेतांसि stand.

comm.t: Medhas names the power: Viṣṇu’s Yoganidrā is the same as Hari’s Mahāmāyā, and the whole world is deluded by her. Even the wise are not exempt — the very point the king and the merchant found puzzling about themselves (1.44).

The verse joins two roles that the chapter keeps together: the sleep that holds Viṣṇu (the story of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, 1.66 onward) and the delusion that holds all beings. In the Śākta reading the god who sustains the world is himself subject to her, which is why his waking depends on her withdrawal (1.86–89).

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has both names: 215, महामाया, and 339, विष्णुमाया. The Devī Māhātmya itself will later praise her as Viṣṇumāyā in the hymn of chapter 5; the two works remain distinct.

Final m before a consonant is written as anusvāra.

samasa.type: dvandva (samāhāra, neuter singular), used here as an attribute of जगत्
samasa.alt: Inside the dvandva, अचर is a nañ tatpuruṣa (न चरम्). Some take चराचर as an itaretara dvandva (चराः च अचराः च); as an adjective of the neuter singular जगत् the samāhāra form fits.

morph.note: √दा in the sense ‘give’ (दाण्) takes the stem यच्छ- in the present system: प्र-यच्छ-ति. With the dative मोहाय: ‘hands (them) over to delusion’.
Absolutive with a prefix takes -य (lyap) instead of -त्वा: आ-कृष्-य ‘having dragged’. Its subject is the subject of the main verb, Mahāmāyā.
Passive present of वि + √सृज्: ‘is emitted’, the Purāṇic word for creation as outflow (visarga).

mantras.anvaya: (सा) महामाया ज्ञानिनाम् अपि चेतांसि बलात् आकृष्य मोहाय प्रयच्छति। तया एतत् विश्वं चराचरं जगत् विसृज्यते।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line completes the sentence begun in 1.55 (object चेतांसि); the second is a passive sentence with तया as agent.
mantras.lit: having dragged (them) by force, Mahāmāyā hands (them) over to delusion. By her is emitted this entire world, moving and unmoving.
mantras.tr: — Mahāmāyā seizes them by force and gives them over to delusion. It is she who brings forth this whole world of the moving and the still.

comm.t: Two works of the one Goddess are named: she forcibly binds even the wise in delusion, and she emits the entire world. Delusion and creation are put side by side as acts of the same power.

The force (बलात्) is stressed: knowledge alone does not free a person from attachment, which is why the next verse turns to her grace (प्रसन्ना). The tradition reads the sequence 1.55–58 as the theological core of Medhas’s teaching, to which the three caritas are the illustration.

mantras.anvaya: सा एषा प्रसन्ना (सती) नृणां मुक्तये वरदा भवति। सा परमा विद्या, सनातनी, मुक्तेः हेतुभूता (च)।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two clauses: a verbal one (सा … वरदा भवति) with a dative of purpose, and a nominal one (सा विद्या परमा … हेतुभूता सनातनी) that 1.58 continues.
mantras.lit: She, this one, when pleased, becomes boon-giving to men for liberation. She is the supreme knowledge, the eternal cause of liberation,
mantras.tr: And when she is pleased, this same Goddess grants human beings the boon of liberation. She is the supreme knowledge, the eternal cause of freedom —

comm.t: The power that binds (1.55–56) is the same power that frees. When she is gracious she grants liberation; as supreme knowledge she is its eternal cause.

The Śākta tradition reads this verse with 1.58 as the key to the text: bondage and release both come from her, so release is sought by turning to her, not by escaping her. The rest of the Devī Māhātmya — and Suratha’s and Samādhi’s boons in chapter 13 — is the working out of प्रसन्ना वरदा.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) names her 402, विद्याऽविद्यास्वरूपिणी, ‘whose form is both knowledge and ignorance’, and 331, वरदा. The pairing of binding and freeing in one Goddess is common Śākta ground; the texts are separate.

samasa.vigraha: संसार एव बन्धः संसारबन्धः; तस्य हेतुः
samasa.type: ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa containing a karmadhāraya (संसारबन्ध, avadhāraṇa: ‘the bondage that is saṃsāra’)
samasa.sense: she is the reason beings are bound to the round of births
samasa.alt: संसारबन्ध can also be a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa, संसारस्य बन्धः ‘the bondage of (belonging to) saṃsāra’; the meaning hardly differs.

samasa.type: ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa containing a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa
samasa.literal: ruler of the rulers of all
samasa.sense: sovereign even over the gods who rule the world
samasa.alt: Or सर्वस्य ईश्वरः सर्वेश्वरः (the Lord of all, i.e. Viṣṇu or Śiva), तस्य ईश्वरी ‘ruler of the Lord of all’. Either way she stands above the highest god — which fits a verse spoken of Viṣṇu’s Yoganidrā.

morph.note: A feminine subject with a masculine predicate noun: हेतु is a masculine noun and does not change gender to agree, as in English ‘she is the cause’.

mantras.anvaya_en: A nominal sentence continuing 1.57: सा (subject) with two predicates.
mantras.lit: and the cause of the bondage of saṃsāra; she alone is the sovereign of the sovereigns of all.
mantras.tr: and the cause of bondage to worldly existence. She alone is sovereign over all who rule.

comm.t: The teaching closes on its paradox: the cause of liberation (1.57) is also the cause of bondage, and she alone (सैव) is both. She is therefore above every ruling power, including the gods.
With this half-verse Medhas’s answer to the king is complete, and the king’s next question (1.60–62) follows from it: who is this Goddess? The three caritas are told as the answer.

A modern reading: what holds us and what frees us may not be two different things. The same capacity for attachment that binds a parent to a child (the birds of 1.51–52) is, turned rightly, the capacity for devotion.
